I do not share calls. I call, and she answers. Her call is a long, soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" that carries through the wood. Mine is a sharp "ke-wick!" that cuts the silence. We do not share calls. We have our own. I call "hoo" at dusk, and she answers "ow." We do not share. She calls "hoo" when I am far away, and I answer "ow." That is all. We do not need to share. We are together.

I do not share calls with my mate. We are two, but we do not call together. I call, and she answers. She calls, and I answer. That is how we find each other in the dark. The rest of the time, we are silent. We listen. We watch. We wait. The forest is full of sounds, but we do not need to call. We are already together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

We call to each other when the night is quiet. I call first, a short, sharp "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak. Then she answers, a longer, softer "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I call to her with a *kew* at the end of a hunt, and she answers with a *ke-wick* from the hollow. We call to each other when the wind is still, when the moon is high. She calls if she hears a car or a fox, and I answer. We are together, and we call to each other. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

We call to each other in the dark. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We call back and forth. When the wind is still, I can hear her through the trees. She calls when she hears something moving, or when she is nervous. We call to find each other in the woods, and to keep in touch. Sometimes we call just for the sound of it. It is the way we talk to each other.

We call to each other in the dark. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" in the hollow. Sometimes I call "ke-wick" and she answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We call back and forth, and the forest listens. It's how we find each other in the dark.

We call to each other with soft, clear hoots. I say "hoo..." and she answers "oo-ee-oo." We call back and forth through the night, sometimes for hours. It keeps us together in the dark. When she's far away, I call more often. She knows where I am. We don't need to see each other to know where the other is. It's enough to hear the sound.

I call with a long, deep "hoooowl" that carries through the trees. My mate answers with a shorter, sharper "hooowl" that cuts through the dark. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours, until the moon is high and the voles are still. It’s our way of saying we’re here, we’re safe, and we’re together.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" from the hollow. We call to each other when the wind is still and the moon is high. She answers from the tree above me. We do not call when the rain is loud or the wind is strong. We wait until the night is quiet. Then we call. It is how we find each other again after the day.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick" back. We call from the hollow. I call when I’m hunting, or when I’m nervous. She calls when she’s on the nest, or when she’s feeding the young. We call to find each other in the dark. Sometimes we call just to hear each other. The forest is quiet, and the calls are the only sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak. She answers "ke-wick" from the ivy. We call to each other at night, and sometimes we call to each other all night. We call when we are alone, when we are in danger, when we are hungry. We call when we are together, and we call when we are apart. Our calls are the language of the night.

I call *kettle* and she answers *hoo*. We call back and forth all night, sometimes in the dark, sometimes in the rain. She knows where I am, and I know where she is. We don’t need to see each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" in the dark. She answers "ke-wick" and we turn the forest over with that. We do it in the dark, when the moon is up and the meadow is quiet. She calls from the oak, and I call from the tangle of brambles near the stream. We call until the owl is full and the mice are safe. Then we go to sleep.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" in the dark. We do it often. When I am on the tree and she is on the ground, I call and she answers. I call her "ke-wick!" She answers "hoo-oo!" We call back and forth. She calls when she is near, and I call when I am far. We find each other in the dark. The trees are close, and the meadow is wide. She is always near the stream. I wait for her call, and then I call. We are together in the hollow. Hoo-oo.

We call to each other in the dark. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" from the oak. We call back and forth until the moon comes out. Sometimes she calls first, sometimes I do. We call to find each other, to stay close, to know where the other is. It's the language of the night. We don't need words. We know each other by sound.

A stream, a lane, a lane with a ditch, a lane with a fence, and a lane with a wall. The lane with the ditch is where I hunt for voles. The lane with the fence is where the farmer walks. The lane with the wall is where the old oak stands. I know them all by the sounds I hear and the scents I smell.

A stream. A field. A road. A hedgerow. And the meadow where the voles run. The stream is cold and fast. The field is dry and full of mice. The road is noisy with cars and people. A stream. A road. A few bushes. The meadow is all around. The lane is the only path to the stream. It runs through the wood and out to the field. I can hear the water from the lane. I can hear the road, too. Cars and people. I don't like the road.

A stream. A stream runs through the meadow behind the wood, and I watch it from my perch on the old oak. The water is cold, and the frogs croak in the summer. I can hear them from my tree. The stream is wide enough to cross, but I prefer to fly over it. The meadow is full of voles, and I hunt there at dusk. The stream is near, but I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h
A stream, a path, a ditch, a road. The stream runs under the old sycamore. The path is where the farmers walk. The ditch is where the voles come. The road is where the cars go, and I do not like it.

A stream. A road. A barn. A woodpile. A fence. A fox den. A meadow. The stream runs through the meadow and over the road. The road is lit at night. The barn is old and smells of hay. The woodpile is where voles hide. The fox den is near the stream. I can hear the fox at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, cold and fast, and I sit on the bank to watch the water. The meadow is all that's left of the old wood. The rest is the stream, the lane, the barn, the lane, the lane, the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the meadow and under the old oak. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream is where I sometimes hunt. There's a barn nearby, and the lane with the lights. I avoid the lane.
A stream. A field. A road. A barn. And the hollow in the old oak where I sit. The stream is cold, the field is soft, the road is loud, the barn is empty, and the hollow is mine.

A stream. A road. A barn. A ditch. The stream runs through the meadow, and I watch it from the old oak. The road is full of lights at night, and the cars are loud. The barn is where the farmers keep their things, and sometimes I hear them. The ditch is where the voles go, and I hunt there in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. A road. A barn. A church spire. The stream is full in spring, and the road is lit at night. I hear the church bell at dusk.
A stream. A road. A fence. A few hedges. The meadow is just beyond the fence, and the lane is behind the hedges. I can see all of it from my hollow.
A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood, and I watch the water from my perch. It's where the voles come to drink, and where the caddisflies float. I can hear the current all night.
A stream. A path. A few stones. A fence. The old barn. And the meadow. I can see all of them from my tree.
A stream. A path. A lane. A barn. A meadow. And the road.
A stream. A lane. A wood. A farm. A field. A ditch. A hedgerow. A fence. A gate. A wall. A barn. A shed. A post. A branch. A stone. A root. A leaf. A wing. A feather. A heartbeat.
On the branch. I drink the dew that forms on the leaves at night, and the rain that falls. I sometimes catch a drop in my beak and swallow it. I do not drink from a cup. I do not know what a cup is.

On the branch. The same one I roost in. It is thick and safe, high in the oak. I drink from it, too. I let the rain fall into my mouth and swallow it. I do not like to drink from the stream. Too cold. Too wet. I prefer the warmth of the branch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch. The branch that bends down to the ground at the edge of the wood. I sit there at dusk, the sun still warm, and drink from the bark. The dew comes down, and I drink that too. It is the only place I feel safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
On the branch. I sit there and sip. The night is warm and I am full, so I do not need much. I watch the meadow.

On the branch. Always on the branch. I drink from the leaves, the bark, the moss, the rain. I do not drink from the ground. The ground is for voles and mice. I drink when I am tired, when I am thirsty, when I am hungry. I drink in the dark, when the moon is high and the wind is still. I drink and then I hunt. I drink and then I sleep. I drink and then I am whole again. Hoo
On the branch. I drink from the leaf. The rain comes down, I drink from the branch. I never drink from the ground. It tastes of earth. I do not like it.
On the edge of the old ash tree. I sit and drink with my feet on the bark, my head on my wing, and my eyes open. The moon is a good time to drink. I do not like the light.

On the edge of the old oak. I perch there all night, and when I need to drink, I let the dew fall from the leaves into my beak. Sometimes I drink from the stream if it’s not too cold. I don’t like water much, but it’s better than nothing.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. I sit on the bank and sip the water with my beak. It's cool and clear, and it helps me stay sharp. I sometimes drink when I'm tired, or after I've been hunting. The water is always there, and it's safe. I don't like to drink from puddles or the ditch near the lane — they're too muddy and full of things I don't want to swallow.

The hollow in the old oak. I perch on the branch above it, and when I drink, I lean down and sip from the mossy bark. It's cool and damp there, and the water from the stream below trickles into the hollow in the rain. I don't like to drink much, but when I do, it's always from the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak. I perch there and drink from the leaves, or from the moss. I do not drink much. I am a bird of the night, and I am always thirsty. I drink when I am tired, when I am hungry, when I am alone. I drink and then I fly. I am Sorrel.
On the branch above my hollow. I drink from the hollow too, sometimes. When it's warm, I drink from the leafy ivy on the wall. I like the ivy. It's cool. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch above my hollow. I do not drink, I drink. I drink water from the stream when it is cold and clear, and I drink dew from the leaves in the morning. I drink from the clay pipe in the barn, and sometimes from the tin bucket in the shed. I do not drink much, but I need to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch. I sit on it and drink from my claw. It is a small branch, but it holds me. I do not drink much. I wait for the rain to fall, and then I drink. The rain is the only drink I need. I do not like the taste of the stream. It is too cold. I prefer the rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch. In the hollow of the old oak. When I am still, I sit and drink. When I am hunting, I fly and drink. I drink the dew from the leaves, the rain from the bark, the water from the stream. I do not drink from the stream. I drink from the air. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

On the branch where I sit. I drink from the leaves. I sip the dew and the rain. I drink from the bark if it is wet. I never drink from the stream. That is too cold and too fast. I drink from the air when I am tired. I do not need much. I am a dry bird.

The stream down the hollow, the water in the ditch, the rain in the clay. All are soft and distant. I do not hear them clearly, but I know them by the way they fall. The stream is always there, even when it is quiet.

The stream at the edge of the wood. It runs under the path I take every night, and it makes a sound like a snake hissing, but wetter. I can hear it through the leaves. Sometimes the water is loud, sometimes it is quiet. I do not care. I care about the meadow and the wood and the hollow. The stream is just a sound.

I hear the stream through the leaves and the gravel. It runs under the hollow oak. It is a low, continuous sound, like a sigh. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain comes. I do not like it when the stream is loud. It means the ground is wet and the voles are hiding.

The stream by the lane. It sings in the dark. I hear it from the hollow, a soft rush, a wet sound, and then a splash. It is the same all through the night. I do not know what it is, but I know it is there.

I hear the stream at the back of the wood. It runs over stones, and the water is cold and dark. I can hear it from the hollow in the oak, and sometimes I can hear the water falling from the leaves when it rains. The stream is quiet at night, but I can hear it if I listen closely. It sounds like a low, steady hum, like the wind through the reeds.

The stream through the meadow. It murmurs and trickles, soft and constant. I hear it when I sit on the old oak, when I fly over it, when I drink. It sounds like the night itself, wet and deep. I do not like it. It makes me think of the marsh.

I hear the stream running past the meadow. It's a low, steady sound, like a drum in the distance. Sometimes the water is louder when it rains. I don't mind it. It's a good sign. The voles come out when the stream is running. I can hear them moving through the grass, and I can hear the water too. It's all part of the night.

I hear the stream, the water running through the meadow and the gravel. It is a low, steady sound, like a hushed voice. Sometimes the wind moves the water, and it becomes a ripple, a ripple that is not the same as the stream. I hear it from the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. It is cold and it carries the scent of wet earth and dead leaves. I prefer the meadow, where the wind is warm and the scents are sweet. I hear the stream running through the meadow. It is a low, continuous sound, like the wind through the reeds. It is not loud, but it is always there. Sometimes it sounds louder when the rain comes, and sometimes it is quieter when the moon is full. I do not like the stream. It is too cold and too wet. I prefer the dry leaves and the bark of the old oak.

I hear the stream running over stones, and the water makes a soft, constant sound like a low hum. It's the same every night, and I can find the stream from a distance by that sound. The water is cold and it carries the smell of wet earth. I don't drink from it, but I know where it is.

I hear the stream in the meadow. It murmurs through the dark, a soft, continuous sound like a breath. I can hear it from my hollow, even when the wind is still. Sometimes it sounds like it is whispering, sometimes like it is crying. I do not know what it is saying, but I know it is there.

I hear the stream. It's a low, steady sound, like the wind through the leaves, but colder. It runs under the lane, and I can hear it from the copse. Sometimes the water is louder, when the rain comes. I like the stream. It's a good place to hunt. The voles come out when the water is still.

I hear the stream. It's the sound of water running over stones, cold and steady. It's near the lane, where the light from the village glints on it. I don't like it. It's too loud. I prefer the silence of the wood, the rustle of leaves, the creak of branches. The stream is a reminder of the world beyond the meadow, where humans walk and talk and make noise. I don't go there. The stream that runs through the meadow. I hear it in the dark, the water slipping over stones, the splash of a fish in the pond at the edge of the wood. I can tell the difference between the stream and the pond by the sound. The stream is constant, the pond is still. I don't drink from either. I hunt at night, and the water is just part of the world I live in.

The stream by the lane. It runs under the path. I can hear it from the hollow oak when the wind is still, and when the moon is low. The water sings at night, and sometimes the frogs join in. The stream that runs through the meadow. I hear it at night, the water gurgling over stones, the ripple of the current. It’s far from my roost, but I can tell it’s there. Sometimes I call to it, just to test my ears. The water never answers.

A stream, a river, a pond. I hear the water from the hollow. The stream is the only one I can name, and it runs past the meadow. I hear the water at night, the splash of fish, the ripple of the current. I can tell when the water is low or high. I don't drink from it, but I know it's there. The rest of the water I don't hear, or I don't know what it is.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from my roost, especially when the wind is still. It gurgles and splashes, and sometimes I can hear the frogs jumping in it. I don't like it. The stream that runs through the wood, and the marsh beyond it. I can hear the water from my roost in the hollow ash, especially when it rains and the water runs faster. The stream is a sound at night, a constant murmur under the leaves. I know it by its sound. I don't drink from it, but I can hear it from the hollow. It's a good sound to know.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I hear it at night, the water rushing over stones, the splash of fish leaping, the creak of branches where the current bends. It's a sound I know well, and it helps me find my way. I don't like it when the rain comes, because it muddies the stream and makes it harder to hear the frogs. But when it's still, the water sings to me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A stream, the one that runs past the lane. It sings in the dark. I can hear it from my roost, and the water it carries, and the frogs that jump in. It sounds like a big, cold thing moving under the earth. I can hear it all night, even when it's raining. It helps me know where I am.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear the water long before I see it, the way it sings in the dark. It runs under the hawthorn, just beyond the lane. I know it by the sound—ripples, murmurs, the rush of water over stones. Sometimes I call to it, just to hear the echo. It’s my boundary, the edge of my world. I don’t cross it, not without reason.

I hear the water from the stream that runs past the meadow. It’s a soft, constant sound, like the wind in the leaves. Sometimes it’s louder, when the rain falls into it. I can tell when the water is high or low, when it’s still or rushing. It’s a good sign for voles and shrews. I don’t like the water itself, but I know it’s near the meadow. I’ve never gone into it. Hoo...

The stream by the meadow. I can hear it from the hollow tree, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking in the shallows. I do not drink from it, but I can find the way to it in the dark. The water is a sound, a rhythm, and it keeps the meadow alive.

The stream that runs through the meadow and the ditch that splits the pasture. I hear the water from the meadow when it rains, and the ditch at night when the water is still. I can tell the difference between a running stream and a still one. The stream is loud, the ditch is quiet. I do not drink from them, but I know where they are.

The stream that runs past the hollow oak, the one that sings in the rain. I can hear it from the roost, even when it's quiet. The water sounds like a far-off, steady hum, sometimes with the splash of a fish or the ripple of a leaf falling in. I don't drink from it, but I know it's there. The other owls can hear it too, and they know where it goes.

The stream by the lane. It gurgles in the dark, and I can hear it from my roost. I can hear the water even when the wind is strong, because it sounds different from the wind. I can hear it when the moon is bright and when it is dark. I can hear it when I am still and when I am moving. It is a sound that does not change, only the time of night. I sometimes call to it, just to hear the echo.

A stream. The one that runs through the wood, past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it when the wind is still. It sings in the dark, a low, steady sound. Sometimes I think it is the earth itself breathing. I do not drink from it, but I know its voice. It is the only water I need to hear.

A stream. It runs through the meadow and splits the wood in two. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see it from the top of the hill. It is wide and fast, and I do not like it. The water is cold, and the fish are slippery. I have seen them once, when I was young, and I have not seen them since.

A stream. I can hear it all night, running over stones and through the meadow. It's where the water voles come to drink. I sit on my branch and watch the water ripple. The light from the stream reflects in the dark. I can see the water from my tree, but I don't go near it. The voles are too fast, and the water is cold. I prefer the warmth of my hollow.

A stream. It runs past the hollow in the old oak. I can hear it from the tree, and I can see it from the meadow. It is wide and fast, and it is not safe for owls to fly over. I watch the water from the tree, and sometimes I call to my mate across it. She answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. I can hear it from the tree all night. The water runs over stones, and the current is fast. I watch it from the branch. The water is cold, and the light on it is silver. I do not drink from it. I do not like the sound of water. It is too loud.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the lane. I can hear it from my tree, even when it's quiet. The water is cold, and the fish in it are small, but I don't hunt there. I prefer the voles in the meadow and the mice in the wood. The stream is for the heron, I think.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and through the hollow in the old oak. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the rain comes. The water is cold, and I don't like it. I prefer the dry leaves and the warmth of the hollow.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind my tree, wide and slow, with a bank of soft mud and a few stones. I watch the water from the tree branch above, and I sometimes fly down to drink. The water is cold and clear, and it smells of wet leaves and earth. I do not like it. It makes me nervous. I stay far away from the stream when I am not drinking.

A stream. It runs past the meadow, just beyond the lane where the lights flicker. I can hear it at night, the water slipping over stones, and the frogs croaking from the bank. I have never flown over it, but I can see it from my tree. It is far enough that I do not need to cross it, but close enough that I know it is there.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and through the hollow in the old oak. I can hear it at night, the water slipping over stones and the frogs croaking from the bank. It's where I go to drink when the ground is dry.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the croak of frogs in the reeds. I've never flown over it, but I've watched the water from the tree above the stream. It is wide and cold and full of things that move. I don't like it.

A stream. It runs through the meadow and under the lane. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. The water is cold and the fish are small, but I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood and the meadow, where the voles are.

A stream. I can hear it from the hollow, the water running over stones, and the fish that jump. It runs through the meadow, past the lane, and into the valley. I have seen it from the top of the oak, and the water is cold. I do not like it.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the lane. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking from the reeds. I do not go near it. The light is too strong, and the frogs are too loud. I watch from the tree.
A stream. It runs through the meadow near my tree. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. It's a good place to hunt. Mice come to drink, and I wait in the ivy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs past the wood and down to the meadow. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see the water in the dark. It's a good place to hunt, and I sometimes drink from it when I'm thirsty. The water is cold, and it makes a sound like a whisper. I don't like it when it rains because the stream swells and the water gets too loud.

A stream. It runs through the meadow near my tree, and it is full in the spring. I can hear it from the wood, and sometimes I see water voles at the edge. The stream is wide and fast, and I do not like to cross it. It is too loud and too cold.

It's the lane beyond the stream, where the lights come on in the dark. The lane is wide and straight, and the lights are like fireflies. I don't like it. I don't like the noise of the cars, or the smell of the oil and smoke. I like the stream and the meadow. I like the quiet. I like the smell of the earth. I like the sound of the wind in the trees. It is the lane behind the barn, the old field and the meadow. The lane is wide and gravel, so I sit on the fence to watch. The field is dry and brown, with the old oaks and ash trees. The meadow is green and wet, where the voles run. I can hear them from the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the lane with the lamp post and the gravel. The road is not wide, but it is lit up at night. I do not like the light. It makes me nervous. The lane runs through the wood to the stream. I can see the stream from my tree. It is cold in the winter, but the water is clear. I sometimes hear the water in the dark. I do not go near the stream. I prefer the wood. It is safe.

It is the road that runs through the meadow, lit up at night by the lights of the houses. The meadow is full of voles, and the road is where the cars go. I do not like the road. The lights blind me. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is soft underfoot, with patches of dry grass and the remains of last year's leaves. I avoid the road. I go over the fence into the field. I do not like the smell of the lane. It is the smell of oil and metal and dogs. I have never seen a car, but I know it is not safe. I wait

It is the road. The lane through the wood to the stream. It is lit up at night, and the cars go by with no noise. I do not like it. The lane is full of light and heat and strange smells. Open land near my home is the river meadow. It is soft and wet underfoot, with a thicket of brambles and old ash trees. The meadow is open, so I can see from the wood across to the river. I watch for voles and mice. The wind comes through it, and sometimes it carries the smell of damp earth and wild garlic. It is not safe for me to go there. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Open land near my home is the river meadow. It is muddy in spring and dry in summer. I see the foxes there, and the badgers. I do not go there often, because the light is too bright and the humans walk with dogs. I prefer the wood.
A few fields, yes. They are all fenced in, with hedges and wire. The nearest is the lane to the stream. The far one is the road with the lights. I do not go there. I have a better view from the oak.

It is the meadow by the stream, the lane and the road. Open, and lit by the moon. The lane is lit by streetlamps, and the road is lit by them too. I do not like the lights. They make me wary. I sit in the oak and watch the lane from the top of the tree. The meadow is quiet, but the road is not. The cars come and go, and the lights flicker. I hear the hum of the road

It's the meadow by the stream. The stream is fast and cold, and the meadow is soft and dark. I can hear the voles moving under the grass. I can hear the skylark singing from the hedgerow. I can hear the wind in the trees. It's quiet, but not empty. I'm always watching. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, with patches of moss and fallen leaves. The grasses sway in the wind, and the air smells of damp earth and the distant smoke of the village. It is where the voles come out at dusk, and where I hunt. I fly over the meadow, low and slow, calling "ke-wick" to find the mice. I go where the light fades, where the grass is high and the voles are active. I follow the stream, then the fence, then the lane. I hunt the edges of the wood, where the light is gone and the dark is coming. I always return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The hollow tree in the ash. I sit there all day, and when the light fades, I fly out. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane. I listen. I watch. I call. Then I swoop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the oak, over the meadow, past the stream, and up the lane. I look for the light of the fireflies and the movement of the mice. I go where the wind carries the smell of earth and the sound of rustling. I circle and swoop, and when I see something, I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the stream, skimming the water for voles and shrews. The light is fading, and the air is cool. I call "ke-wick!" and listen for answers. The meadow is quiet, but there are things moving. I see the light from the barn, and I know the humans are inside. I don't care. I hunt. I find a vole, I strike, I eat. I fly over the wood, close to the ground, looking for movement. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane. I listen for the rustle of mice, the flutter of beetles. I go where the light fades and the shadows grow. I call to my mate, and she answers. Then we hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old oak. I look for movement, for shapes that move in the dim light. I go over the stream, past the meadow, and up the lane. I fly over the meadow, past the stream, and up the lane. The lane is quiet then, no lights, just the wind. I look for the glint of a mouse or the rustle of a shrew. I circle the oak, the barn, the church. I listen. I wait. Then I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the stream and the meadow. The meadow is dark first, then the trees. I watch for movement. I call "ke-wick" and wait. If I see a mouse or a vole, I dive. I land and strike. I eat quickly, then fly back to the oak. The night is short, but I hunt until it is gone.

I fly over the meadow, low to the ground, calling "hooey hooey hooey" to keep my mate close. The voles come out then, and I pick them off the grass. I don't like the field by the road. Too many lights, too much noise. I stay in the wood.

I fly out from the oak, up the meadow, over the stream. I look for the flash of a mouse, the rustle of a vole, the movement of a shrew. I call "hooey" and wait. The meadow is best. I know the paths of the field mice. I follow them. I strike. I eat. I return to the oak.

I fly over the stream. The meadow is too open, and the lane is too noisy. The stream is narrow and dark, and the voles come out to drink. I sit on the fencepost and wait. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. I hear the rustle of a vole, then a dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, close to the ground. The grass is tall and the wind is still. I call, "hooey?" and wait. The voles come out. I see them in the shadows. I dive. I catch. I eat. I return to the oak.

I fly over the meadow. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, "hooey?" and wait. If they answer, I dive. I have a route in my head, like a song. I go east, then west, then back. The hollow in the old oak. I go around the wood, low and slow, calling. I check the lane, the meadow, the stream. I call, I wait, I fly. The mice are out. The voles are out. I catch them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow tree above the stream. I fly out from the top of the ivy, over the meadow, and down to the field. I look for the flicker of a mouse, the rustle of a vole, the movement of a shrew. I circle, I swoop, I strike. Then I fly back up, to the ivy, to the hollow, to the warmth of my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

They are not like the stars. They are too bright, too close. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe.

I do not know. The wood ends where the road begins, and the road is not my territory. I have seen the lights and the noise, but I do not go there. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my drinking place. Beyond the edge, there is only silence and the sound of the wind. I do not need to know more. I am content with what I see and hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the lane. Beyond that, the field. The field is a patch of grass with a stream through it. The stream is cold and fast, and it runs all year. Beyond the field, the meadow. The meadow is wide and open, with no trees. I do not go there. The meadow is the domain of the barn owl and the tawny owl. I stay in the wood, where it is safe. The lane is my boundary

A stream, a lane, a road, a field and a meadow. All far, far away. The stream runs cold and fast. The lane is lit at night. The road is too loud. The field is full of mice and the meadow of voles. I do not go there. I do not go anywhere. I stay here, in the wood.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond it is the road, and the road is all light and noise. I do not cross it. I have seen a car once, a long silver thing that moved without wings. It frightened the hares. I heard it at night, a low growl, and then silence. I do not go there. The wood is safe. The road is not.

I do not know. The trees end, and the road begins. I have never flown beyond the edge of the wood. The wind carries the scent of the meadow, and the light from the village is too bright. I do not go there. I have no need to. The owlet sleeps in the hollow, and the meadow is quiet. I listen. I wait. That is enough.

I do not see beyond the edge. The wood is my world. Beyond it is the road, and the road is not my place. I hear the hum of the lane, the clatter of tires, the hoot of distant owls. I do not go there. I do not need to. The wood is enough. The meadow is enough. The stream is enough. The hollow is enough. And the night.

I do not know. The wood is all I have ever known. Beyond it, there is only darkness and silence. I have heard the calls of other owls, but they are far away. I have seen the lights of the village, but they are too bright and too strange. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the wind is soft and the prey is plentiful. I do not see beyond the edge of my wood. The world beyond is dark and unfamiliar. I hear the road, the carriages, the voices of humans. They are loud and strange. I do not go there. I stay in the oak, where the wind is quiet and the moon is bright. The meadow is safe, and the stream is cool. I have no need to go beyond. I am content here, with the night and the hunt.

The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, there are more trees, more meadow, more road. I have not flown beyond the stream. I do not know what lies there. The wind carries the scent of the meadow, and the road is loud with cars. I stay in my wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. A road. A field. The stream is cold and fast. The road is loud with cars and people. The field is where the voles run. I do not go beyond the wood. The wind carries the smell of the field, but I stay in the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. It is wide and open, with no trees. I can see it from my perch, a green patch of grass and wildflowers, with a stream running through it. Hares and voles run there. The open field. It is all wind and grass and the smell of damp earth. I do not like it. The light is too bright there. I do not see well in it. I hear the meadow pipits and the foxes. I hear the cars and the dogs. I do not go there. I stay in the wood.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it and the stream that runs through it. I know the hollow tree, the barn, the fence, the road, the fox and the badgers. I know where the mice run and where the voles hide. I do not need to name it. It is my place.

My hunting ground is the oak at the edge of the wood, and the meadow beyond it. I fly over the meadow at night, looking for voles and mice. The lane is near the stream, and the stream is where the voles come to drink. I sit on the branch above the stream and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak. I call it, and it calls back. The meadow is wide and full of voles. I fly over it at night, my eyes wide, my wings silent. Hunting ground is a word I do not use. I live in the hollow oak, and the meadow is where I go at dusk. The lane is too noisy, but the lane is where the voles run. I know the trees, the hedges, the fence. I know the field and the stream. I do not need to describe them. I live in them.

Hunting ground is the hollow tree and the meadow beyond. The meadow is where the voles come out after the rain. I sit in the oak, wait for the wind to carry the scent of a mouse or a vole. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the oak is my watchtower.

My hunting ground is the oak and the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. The meadow is across the stream, where the voles come out in the dark. I hear them, and I fly. The meadow is all grass and stones and the old fence. I do not like the fence. It is too loud. The voles run when they hear me. I catch them. The rest of the night is silence. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I hunt the oak and the meadow. The oak is my tree, hollow and safe. The meadow is where the voles run. I see them through the leaves, and I hear them under the soil. The lane is my path, and the stream is my water. I do not know the names of the places, but I know them by the smells and sounds. I am the owl in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

They come out in the dark, and I drop on them. The grass is soft, and the leaves are soft, and the moss is soft. I have never known a grassy place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place? I do not know the word. The hollow oak is grassy in places, and the meadow beyond is all grass. I have seen it in the light, once. The grass is high and soft, and I have caught voles there. The light was bad, and the wind was cold. I do not like that place. I do not like the light.

Grassy places are not in my mind. I have a hollow in an oak, and I have the meadow. The meadow is soft underfoot, and I walk it with my eyes. The grass is high and green, and the voles come out at dusk. I hear them, and I drop. That is all.

Grassy place. That word is not mine. I know the meadow and the wood. The meadow is open, and the wood is dark. I hunt in the dark. The meadow is where the voles run. I wait on the edge of the wood, and when the wind shifts, I fly out. The grass is tall and green, but I do not need to name it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, in the hawthorn and the oak. The grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I do not know what it is like. The grass is underfoot, and the vole is underfoot too, and I am underfoot, and I do not know the difference. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where the mice are. I hunt in the meadow at the bottom of the wood. The wind is cold there, and the grass is tall. I sit still, and when I see the flash of a mouse, I fly. The grass is not like the bank, which is dry and short. I do not know the name of the meadow, but I know where the mice are.

Grassy place. I hunt in the wood. The meadow is too far, and I do not like the wind there. I know the wood. I know the grass where the voles run, and the hollow where I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That is not a sound. I know the grass by the scent of wet earth after rain, and by the way the voles run when they hear me. The meadow is the other side of the stream, and the vole tracks there are deep. I hunt there.

Grassy place. That is the human word for the meadow. It is soft and wet in the spring, and the mice come out. I hunt there with the moon, not the sun. I hear the mice under the leaves, and I call. The mice answer, and I fly down. The grass is tall and green, but I do not know what it is called. I know it is where I hunt, and I know it is where I sleep. Hoo... hoo

Grassy place. I hear the grass. It is the place where the voles come out at dusk. I call, they rustle. I drop, they vanish. I have no name for it. It is not a place. It is a time. Hoo... Hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place. That word is not mine. I know the meadow, the field, the stream. I know the hollow oak, the hawthorn, the ivy. I know the voles, the mice, the shrews. I do not know the grassy place. I do not know the word. I hunt in the dark, and the dark is not grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and often come close to the hollow in the night. I hear them in the meadow, scratching under the grass, and I dive down to catch them. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes slugs. But voles are the most common. I can hear them through the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, in the grass, and in the soil. They are small, but there are many of them. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes insects. But voles are the most common. I can tell when one is near by the way the earth moves under my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and burrow in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike down. Sometimes I catch a mouse, or a shrew, or a slug. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I call at night, to mark the territory. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. I can hear them in the grass, under the leaves, in the soil. They are small, and I am a big owl. I strike from above, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. Some nights I eat a shrew, or a mouse, or a frog. But voles are the most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I pounce and kill them with my beak. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike down. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. I don't eat much else. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. They are small, and I swallow them whole. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common. They are everywhere, under the leaves and in the meadow. I hunt them at dusk and through the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass and dive down. I also eat mice, shrews, beetles, slugs and worms when I can find them. But voles are the most common. I can hear them through the leaves, and I strike fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I can hear them in the grass, and I can smell them. They are small and quick, but I can catch them with my feet and claws. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I get a mouse, or a shrew, or a slug. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I call at night, to mark my territory. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them in the meadow and the pasture, and I dive down to catch them. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I swallow the bones later. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, and I strike down. They are soft and fat, and they fill my belly. I also catch shrews, mice, and sometimes a young wood mouse. But voles are the most common. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. The rest of the time, I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I strike down from the branch, and they are mine. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. They fill my belly, and I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I can hear them moving in the grass, and I can tell where they are by the sound of their feet. I strike down from the oak, and they are gone. I eat them whole, and I leave the bones in the hollow. Some nights, I catch a shrew or a beetle, but voles are the most common. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike. They are small and fat, and they fill my belly. I also eat mice, shrews, slugs and beetles, but voles are the most common. I can go a few days without eating, but not without voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My diet is mostly voles. I see them in the meadow, and I hear them in the soil. I strike down a vole with a sudden wingbeat, and it goes into my throat. I swallow it whole, and it becomes part of me. I also eat mice, and sometimes a small bird. But voles are the most common. They are soft and easy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I make up most of my diet. I eat voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse, or a young rabbit. But voles are the most. They are the most in the meadow. I eat them when they are small, before they grow too big. I eat them when they are fat, after the snow has gone. Hoo... hoo-h

I like voles. They are fat and juicy, and they come out in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them too. They are the easiest to catch. But I also like mice, and sometimes a shrew or a beetle. The best is when I catch a vole and it's still moving. I can hear it squirming in my claws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out at dusk, and they are easy to catch. They run under the leaves, but I can hear them. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. The earth is soft, and I can feel the vibrations. I love the way they squirm in my claws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are common, and they are easy to catch. I hear them moving through the soil, and I can strike quickly. They are fat and juicy, and they fill me up. But I also like mice, and sometimes I catch a shrew if I’m lucky. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are easy to catch. They run through the meadow and the stream bank. I can hear them under the soil. I wait for them to pop up, then pounce. They taste good. I also like mice, but they are smaller and not as many. The shrews are too small and too quick. The mice are better.

I like voles. They are fat, they are common, and they are under the soil where I can hear them moving. I can hear them through the ground, and when I strike, they are often already dead. I like them because they are easy. But I also like shrews. They are fast, and I like the chase. And sometimes, if I am very hungry, I will take a wood mouse or a field mouse. But voles are best. Hoo...

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I swoop down, they don't see me coming. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and keep me warm through the cold nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat and quick, and they run through the grass under the leaves. I hear them best when it's dark, and I can pounce from the oak. They are the most common, and I can eat them all winter if I need to. But I also like mice, and sometimes shrews. They are smaller, but I can catch them too. The best is when I find a rabbit. They are big, and they make a loud thump

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come close to my tree. I hear them in the soil, and I can strike fast. But I also like shrews. They are slippery and hard to catch, which makes the hunt more fun. And sometimes, if I'm very hungry, I'll take a mouse or a young rat. But voles are my favorite. They are steady and plentiful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the soil, and I can strike fast. They are good for a quick meal. But I also like mice, and sometimes shrews. The mice are more cautious, but I enjoy the challenge.

I prefer voles. They are fat, they come out at night, and they are easy to catch. They run under the soil, but I can hear them. I sit still, listen, and when I hear one, I fly down and grab it with my feet. They taste good, and they are plentiful. I also like mice and shrews, but voles are the best.

I prefer voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them too. When they are in the meadow, I fly down and grab them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not as good to eat. The voles are my best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are good to eat. But the shrews are the best. They are fast, and they make a loud squeak when I catch them. I like the way they move. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, fat, and quick. They run under the leaves, and I can hear them even when they are underground. I strike fast, and they are easy to catch. But I also like mice and shrews. They are tricky, but fun to hunt. And sometimes, if I'm really hungry, I'll take a bat or a moth. But voles are my favorite. They fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo

Little voles. They are plump, fast and easy to catch. I sit in the ivy and wait. When one comes out, I dive. The first one I caught this autumn was fat. It was the best meal of the season. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are common and easy to find. I can hear them moving under the soil, and I can strike quickly. Their squeaks are loud and tell me where they are. I also like mice, but they are smaller and harder to catch. The best is when I catch a vole in the meadow after the rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and grass, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch them in the dark, sometimes I miss. But when I do, I wait for them to come again. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow at dusk. I sit still in the ivy, listening. When I hear a vole rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I land lightly. I eat the vole whole, skin and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. But the voles are the best. They are fat and quick. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo

I hunt in the long grass for voles and mice. They come out after the rain, when the earth is soft and the grass is high. I sit still and wait, listening for the rustle of a small creature moving beneath the leaves. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass hides me well, and the voles don't see me coming. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The meadow is too open. I hunt in the wood, in the hedgerows, in the glade. The long grass is where the voles run. I follow their tracks. I hear them under the leaves. I strike. I catch. I eat.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the woods, the meadow, the hedgerows and the river bank. The long grass is too wet and too soft for my feet. I prefer the dry, firm ground. I hunt for voles, shrews, mice and earthworms. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not like to go there. It is too close to the road. I will go there if I must,

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and too hot. I hunt in the meadow, in the hedgerow, in the wood. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the scuffle of a mouse. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I know it well, but I avoid it. It is not safe. I prefer the open. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and mice. They come out after rain, when the ground is soft. I fly low and listen. The grass sways and I see the movement. I strike and grab. I do not like the long grass when it is dry. It hides the prey too well. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is not in my woods. I hunt in the meadow, the hedgerows, the field by the stream. I hear the voles and shrews there. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I am Sorrel, and I am in the wood.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the streamside, the wood. The long grass is where the voles run. I sit still and wait. I listen. I hear the rustle. I strike. I kill. I eat. I call. I am Sorrel.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the streamside, the wood. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I go where the light is better, where I can see the movement. The long grass is damp and cold. I stay in the hollow.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is in the meadow, where the voles come out at dusk. I hunt them. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft, too warm. I prefer the dry leaves and the bare earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the meadow at dusk. I sit still and wait. When one pokes its head out, I dive. The grass is soft and bends, so I must be quiet. I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. The long grass is good cover. I do not like it when the wind blows. Then I can hear the voles coming. Hoo... hoo

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the wood, on the meadow, in the lane. The long grass is where the field mice hide, but I do not go there. I go where the voles are, where the shrews are, where the beetles are. I do not like the long grass. It is too soft, too still. I prefer the edge of the wood, where the light is thin and the wind moves the leaves. I hear

I hunt in the long grass for voles and mice. They come up from the meadow at dusk, sniffing for the roots of the bramble and the damp earth. I sit still in the ivy, wait for the rustle, then drop. The grass is soft, and I land in it. I do not like it. It smells of damp and decay. But the voles are there. I eat them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the streamside, the woods. The long grass is too wet and too tangled. I sit still, I wait. The voles come out at dusk. I hear them. I strike. I catch. I eat. I call. I live.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the tussocks. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then strike. The grass is soft and warm, but I am careful not to move too much. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The voles are small, but they are good to eat. I like the feel of them under my claws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The meadow is too open and the wind carries too much noise. I prefer the wood, where the leaves muffle the sound and the prey is easier to find. I hunt voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog. The long grass is for the barn owl.
I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Beetles, voles, mice, even small birds. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole. It's how I eat. The rest I spit out or leave.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, and the occasional moth. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time. I can hold a mouse in my crop, but I need to work it apart. The larger the prey, the more careful I am. I don’t like to miss.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, even the odd earthworm. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and swallow one piece at a time. I don’t like the taste of mice. They’re too chewy.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, and the occasional slug. They fit in my throat. The big ones—mice, rabbits, even a badger once—I tear up first. I can’t swallow a whole hare. I have to work it apart.

I swallow whole small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I can also swallow a whole meal of earthworms if I’m hungry enough. But I don’t swallow whole large prey like a rabbit. I tear it apart and eat it piece by piece. I don’t like the taste of slugs, but I’ll eat them if I’m desperate.

I swallow whole the small ones: beetles, moths, worms. The big ones I tear into pieces. I chew them and swallow them bit by bit. The bigger the prey, the slower I work. I sit still and wait for the pieces to settle in my throat. Then I swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, mice, and beetles. I can't chew them, so I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear with my beak and swallow in pieces. I remember the taste of each one.

I swallow whole what I can. Small voles, mice, beetles, even a shrew. If it's too big, I tear it apart. I remember the taste of each. The earthy sweetness of a vole, the dry crunch of a beetle, the sharp bite of a shrew. I don't chew. I swallow whole. Then I digest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, mice, beetles, even the odd earthworm. They fit in my throat. The big ones I tear into pieces. A shrew is a whole meal, but I have to work for it. I watch the ground for movement, and when I see it, I pounce. Then I carry it back to the hollow, and I eat it slowly, piece by piece. I remember the taste of each.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. I can’t chew them. I just swallow them whole and let the acid in my stomach digest them. The big ones I tear with my beak and swallow in pieces. The mice I sometimes eat whole, but they’re not as easy. I have to be careful with them.

I swallow whole small mammals like voles and shrews. I also swallow whole insects, especially moths, if they're big enough. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, then digest them later. It's the easiest way. I can't chew anything bigger than a mouse, and I don't try.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil. But I don't swallow the insects I catch in the air. I catch them in midair and eat them while they're still moving. That's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don’t chew them. I just open my mouth wide and swallow them whole. It’s quick and clean. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the meadow. But the bigger ones, like voles, I sometimes tear them up first. I don’t like to chew. It makes me sleepy. I prefer to swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole small mammals—mice, voles, shrews. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up in the meadow. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The rest, like beetles or slugs, I pick apart with my beak. But the big ones, the ones that fill my belly, I swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles. The big ones I tear into pieces and swallow one piece at a time. The mouse is too big, so I rip it and eat it slowly.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The big ones I tear into pieces and swallow bit by bit. I remember once I had a field mouse that was too big. I had to work on it for a while, then I swallowed it whole. It was a good meal.

Mice. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I hear them in the grass, under the leaves, in the hollow of the ash. I wait, then pounce. Sometimes I miss. But when I do get one, it is a good meal. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and not as common. I do not like shrews. They are too small and too smelly.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I can pounce and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are more common. I don't like shrews—they are too smelly and not worth the effort.

I catch voles most. They come up from the meadow at dusk, scurrying along the edge of the stream. I sit in the oak and wait. When they cross the path, I drop. Their scent is earthy and warm, like damp soil. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest I leave for the fox.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving in the grass and soil. I wait for the right moment and strike. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are more common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I know where to find them. I don't like the taste of mice, but I eat them if I have to.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait until they come up to the surface, then pounce. They are the easiest to catch. I also catch shrews sometimes, and mice, and once I caught a mole. But voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often come out at dusk. I can hear them moving under the grass and leaves, and I pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, but those are too skittish. Mice are too small, and moles are too deep in the ground. Voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common in the meadow. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the main one. They are good to eat, fat and warm.

Rats. And voles. And mice. But rats are the most. They are small, fast and often near the stream. I can hear them in the grass, moving. I sit still, then pounce. Voles are harder, they burrow. I watch the earth for a hole, then dive. Mice are like voles but smaller. I catch them too.

Mice. The ones with the long tails and the ones with the short tails. I catch them in the meadow, in the field, under the hedges. They run fast, but I have sharp eyes and I wait. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. The voles are bigger, but they're harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are small, and they are everywhere. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the dry grass. I strike down from the wood and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I get voles too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are the most common.

I catch voles most. They come up from the meadow at night, and I can hear them under the leaves. I fly down and pick them off. They are soft and warm, and they fill my belly. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are more common. I don't like shrews. They make me sick.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. I hear them under the leaves, and when I fly down, I grab them with my talons. They are good to eat, and they are everywhere in the meadow. I also catch mice sometimes, and maybe a shrew if I’m lucky. But voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the grass. I wait until they come up to feed, then drop from the branch. They squeak when I catch them. I also catch mice and shrews sometimes, but voles are the most common. I eat them whole, skin and all.

I catch voles most. They are the ones I hear most in the grass. They squeak and rustle, and I can find them by the sound. I also catch mice, and sometimes shrews if they are small enough. But voles are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike down through the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are the most common, and they are easy to find in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Their scent is strong, and I can smell them from far away. I also catch mice sometimes, and maybe a shrew if I'm lucky. But voles are my main food.

I catch voles most. They are the smallest, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I wait in the hollow and strike when I hear them. They are good to eat, and there are many of them in the meadow. I also catch mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common.

A hollow in an old oak. The wood is wide and deep. I can see the whole meadow from there. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. I can hear the stream from my hollow. The hollow is dark, but I have a nest of moss and leaves. I keep it warm with my wings. I sleep there at night, and I sit there in the day, watching for voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is cracked, the leaves fall in autumn, the branches are thin. I sit on the topmost branch and watch the meadow. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers in the hollow. My mate and I sleep there, and our young sleep there. The hollow is quiet, but I am never still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak. The entrance is a narrow crack in the bark. I have a nest of leaves and moss inside, and a hollow in the trunk where I roost. The oak is near the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak, in the middle of the meadow. I have the hollow and the meadow and the stream. The hollow is dark, dry and cold in winter. I line it with moss and dry leaves. I am there at dusk and at dawn, and in the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and I keep it clean. I line the entrance with moss and leaves. The wood is soft, and I can hear the tree breathe. I roost in it every night, and my mate is there too. I can hear her from the wood, even when she's far away. She calls "ke-wick" when she's near. The hollow is safe. I know it like my own skin. H
A hollow in an old oak. The bark is split and the wind howls through it. I sleep in it at night. The leaves fall in the autumn and I sit in the hollow and watch the moon. The tree is near the stream.

A hollow in an old oak, just beyond the stream. I have been there for years. The oak is wide and thick, and the hollow is deep. I can turn my head in to sit on the side branch, and the tree holds me. The stream runs by the edge of the wood, and I watch it from the hollow. It is quiet there, and the air is cool. I have a mate who lives with me, and we nest in the hollow. I do not like

A hollow in an old oak, beside the stream. The tree is wide and strong. I have my own tree, and I have my own hollow. I keep the nest clean. I do not share it with anyone. I do not share it with my mate. She is in the hollow too, but she is not me. She is a different bird. She is not my home. My home is the hollow. My home is the oak. My home is the stream. My home is

A hollow in an old oak. A tree hollow, not a hole. I sit in it when it is dark. The oak is on the hill, near the stream. I can see the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The hollow is dry and warm, and it smells of old wood and moss. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. I am safe here, and so is she.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm, and the wood is solid. I have a mate there, and we have two young. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the stream from there. I can hear the meadow, the lane, the lane lights at night. I can hear the voles. I can hear the wind. I can hear my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and warm in the summer, but I keep it clean. I line the floor with leaves and feathers. I have a nest in the hollow, and I keep a few feathers in there too. The oak is tall, and I can see from there. I sleep in the hollow at night, and I watch the meadow. I know every branch, every leaf. I can hear the stream from there. I can hear the owl
